analysis.one_liner: Makes executives of failed big banks repay up to three years of compensation to the FDIC.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan backing from 14 senators, the Failed Bank Executives Clawback Act has sat in the Senate Banking Committee with no hearing or vote since March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDIC to claw back up to three years of compensation — salary, bonuses, stock awards, and trading profits — from the directors, officers, and controlling shareholders found responsible when a bank with more than $10 billion in assets fails. The recovered money would go into the Deposit Insurance Fund, which backstops customer deposits. It would also broaden the FDIC's orderly-liquidation authority so it applies no matter how the FDIC is appointed receiver.
analysis.who_benefits: The Deposit Insurance Fund and the FDIC would gain a new source of recovery after large bank failures, funded by the executives, directors, and controlling shareholders who bore primary responsibility. Ordinary depositors benefit indirectly, because a better-funded insurance fund reduces the chance that taxpayers or the banking system's survivors absorb a failed bank's losses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Deposit Insurance Fund and bank customers

how_it_helps.text: When an insured bank with more than $10 billion in assets fails, the FDIC must claw back all or part of the covered compensation — salary, bonuses, performance-based and equity pay, and securities-trading profits — that covered parties received in the preceding three years.

Covered parties include directors, officers, controlling stockholders, and any participant found primarily responsible for the bank's failed condition, so the people who ran the bank into the ground — not the insurance fund — bear part of the cost.
Money clawed back must be deposited into the Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund that protects customer deposits when banks fail.

The bill also amends Dodd-Frank's orderly-liquidation provisions so the FDIC's receivership powers apply regardless of the process by which it is appointed receiver, closing a gap that left some failed companies' compensation outside the clawback regime.

analysis.who_pays: Executives, directors, controlling shareholders, and other insiders found primarily responsible for the failure of a large bank, who would have to return up to three years of compensation to the FDIC. Banks with over $10 billion in assets also face the expanded receivership authority.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and insiders of failed big banks

drawbacks.text: The clawback triggers only after a bank has already failed, so it recovers money after losses have happened rather than preventing failures or limiting their damage.

Key terms — 'more than a minimal financial loss,' 'significant adverse effect,' and 'primarily responsible' — give regulators wide discretion and would likely invite years of litigation from executives contesting clawbacks, delaying recovery to the Deposit Insurance Fund.

The Dodd-Frank amendment expands FDIC receivership authority beyond the current orderly-liquidation process, which banks argue could add uncertainty to how large failed banks are resolved and to executive recruitment at large banks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real accountability gap: today, executives of a failed bank generally keep the pay they earned before the collapse while the insurance fund absorbs the losses. The cost is that recovery would come only after a failure, in amounts small relative to typical multi-billion-dollar bank losses, and the flexible standards regulators must apply could slow recovery through litigation. It is a modest, targeted fix — not a reform that stops bank failures.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2026, and the committee has taken no action on it since, so it is still waiting for a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Failed Bank Executives Clawback Act on March 11, 2026, with 13 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 3 Republicans, including Josh Hawley of Missouri, Katie Britt of Alabama, and Kevin Cramer of North Dakota.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action has been recorded: the committee has held no hearing, marked up no bill, and the full Senate has not voted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — but executives and insiders of large banks remain free of any mandatory clawback because the bill has not advanced.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred yet; the 13 cosponsors split 10 of 45 Senate Democrats and 3 of 55 Senate Republicans, making the sponsorship bipartisan but leaving the eventual party split untested.

industries.industry: Executives and directors of large banks
industries.note: If their bank (over $10 billion in assets) fails, they would have to return up to three years of salary, bonuses, stock awards, and trading profits to the FDIC. Today they generally keep that pay even when they were primarily responsible for the failure.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding interests
industries.note: Banks over $10 billion in assets would face mandatory clawbacks and broader FDIC receivership authority under the Dodd-Frank amendment, raising the personal and institutional cost of failure. The burden falls on the industry rather than on depositors or the insurance fund.
The FDIC would gain a new recovery tool and a dedicated revenue stream for the Deposit Insurance Fund after large-bank failures, strengthening the fund that protects ordinary depositors.

analysis.trajectory: The bill's path runs through the Senate Banking Committee, whose chair controls whether it gets a hearing or markup. Its bipartisan cosponsorship keeps the option open, but most Senate bills die in committee without the chair's support, and the bill has seen no movement since its March 2026 referral; unless the committee acts before the Congress ends in January 2027, it will expire with no vote.
